description:
Scenario: memory.rs:369-385 (find_uniqueness_conflict) iterates every Metadata object in the account on every create_object call. For O(N) stored objects, every create is O(N) — total cost for N creates is O(N²). Same scan repeats in update_object's post-patch re-check (memory.rs:806-825).

For a 'reference implementation' this is fine. The risk is downstream contributor copy: a contributor who reads the pattern and ports it to their postgres backend may write a 'SELECT * FROM metadata WHERE account_id = ' and then loop in application code to find the conflict, replicating the O(N) scan against the database — when a UNIQUE INDEX would handle the same job in O(log N).

Maintenance consequence: the 'how to do uniqueness in your real backend' is unstated. The MemoryBackend's scan-based approach is what a contributor will see and reach for. The correct pattern (database UNIQUE INDEX or in-memory HashSet<UniquenessKey>) is mentioned nowhere in the rustdoc.

Fix direction: add a 'Notes for production backends' section under the uniqueness bullet (memory.rs:28-33) explicitly stating: 'Production backends should declare a UNIQUE INDEX on (account_id, related_type, related_id, type_name, is_private) — not loop through records'. Also worth filing a separate efficiency bead on the MemoryBackend itself: a HashMap<UniquenessKey, Id> would cut the scan to O(1) at the cost of one extra map. Not necessary for tests, but the explicit O(1) data structure is exactly the kind of thing a contributor should copy.
title: find_uniqueness_conflict is O(n) per create — scales linearly with stored objects, no early-exit data structure
